captions: Each campaign is a network of models and measurements. Each node is a step the lab runs.
Each step's results feed the next. BOFN models every step, not just the final score.
Next: every step as the experiment and the data it makes, for one alloy of each campaign.
FLAIME: aluminium alloys for laser powder bed fusion. A design is aluminium plus up to 8 of 15 alloying elements.
This is design 299 of the replayed run, seed 0: the alloy that took it past the halfway target, on day 96.
ONR: copper alloys designed as powders for blown-powder DED. A design is copper plus up to 6 of 8 elements.
This is design 74 of the replayed run, seed 5: the alloy that took it past the best existing alloy on this synthetic benchmark, on day 221.
CALPHAD runs on the BYU HPC: pycalphad on open databases, Thermo-Calc as an interface. This curve is the open-database node's, the one the optimizer sees.
The same alloy three ways: the node's fast model, a full Scheil run on an open database, and the twin's hidden truth. They differ, as a simulator differs from a real alloy.
From its curve the node reads the liquidus, the freezing range, a hot-cracking index and a growth-restriction factor.
The network's print node takes two of them, the liquidus and the cracking index. The atomizer's melt is set from the same liquidus.
One laser track over the powder bed, shown 10,000 times slower. The colours are the temperature field of the twin's melt-pool model for this alloy.
A point 2 layers down melts again as the track passes over it, then cools through the liquidus at 2.0 million kelvin a second.
The twin takes five numbers from this model: the pool's width and depth, a lack-of-fusion index, a keyhole index and the cooling rate.
This is the twin's stand-in for Thermo-Calc's AM Module, not Thermo-Calc output. No run in round 3b bought this node.
The lab makes its own powder: it doses and presses the charge, atomizes it and checks the powder.
Laser diffraction sizes the powder. This distribution is the twin's simulated measurement of this alloy's lot.
One of three runs failed here. 13 % of the charge ends up in the cut the printer takes: the atomize node's output.
Each powder is printed at several laser settings; every build is checked for density and cracks.
Each cube is weighed in air and in water, then sectioned and imaged. Its density and its crack reading go on the map at its setting.
The tensile blanks are printed at the middle setting. One build gives the network nine rows: settings in, density and cracks out.
One electron beam scans the sample line by line. Each detector catches a different signal from the spot it is on.
Secondary electrons show the surface, backscattered electrons the composition, X-rays the elements, diffraction the crystal's orientation.
Every image here is simulated by the twin for this alloy. The read-outs are the twin's own analysis of those images.
The network uses three of the four: the powder's satellites, the section's pores and cracks, EBSD's grains.
Sections show pores, cracks and grains; PIP reads a stress-strain curve from one indent.
Bars are cut by wire EDM, then heat treated. The twin books the furnace for three hours and models the strength it leaves, not the profile: this one is illustrative.
Then three bars are pulled to fracture. Each curve is the twin's simulated load record for this alloy.
Yield strength and elongation feed the tensile node. The utility scores them against the reference alloys, and counts the mineral burden.
A one-hour corrosion screen ranks the deposits before bars are made and tested.
Two quick scans follow the hour at rest. The network takes the early rate and the breakdown potential.
Then 30 days in seawater, read on days 1, 3, 7 and 14 on the way, and ICP-MS of what dissolved.
The 30-day rate and the selective attack are the immersion node's outputs. A policy may stop a coupon early.
Both campaigns run at once in one lab, sharing its atomizer, SEM, outside facilities, market and calendar.
A node lights up while the lab is running that step.
From here on each node is an icon, lit while its step runs.

placed.text: Each campaign is a function network: a chain of steps, where each step's results feed the next. BOFN, Bayesian optimization over function networks, models every step, not just the final score.
Here is each step itself, for one alloy from each campaign: the experiment, and the data it makes. Everything is simulated by the twin, unless a label says otherwise.
The aluminium alloy is design number 299: aluminium with eight additions, manganese and chromium the largest.
On this map of the search space, it is one of 435 designs the run simulated.
The copper alloy is design number 74: an aluminium bronze, with a little nickel and titanium.
CALPHAD comes first. As the melt cools, a Scheil model follows how much of it has frozen. This curve is the one the optimizer sees.
A full Scheil run on an open database adds the phases as they form. The twin's hidden truth differs again, as a real alloy would.
From its curve, the network takes two numbers: the liquidus, and a hot-cracking index.
Every run in round three b used this open node. The Thermo-Calc stand-in was never bought.
The twin stands in for the AM module with a moving point source of heat. It gives the melt pool's width and depth, and how fast the metal cools.
This is not Thermo-Calc output, and no run bought this node. But the same model decides the porosity of every simulated build.
For aluminium, the lab makes each alloy's powder itself, then prints it and checks every build.
This footage is real: our own atomizer, running a bronze. The size distribution beside it is the twin's, for this alloy.
Here, one of three runs failed, and 13 percent of the charge ended up in the printer's size range.
One build is nine cubes, each at its own laser power and speed.
Each cube's density and crack reading goes on the map. Too little energy leaves lack of fusion. Too much makes keyhole pores.
One build gives the network's print node nine data points.
In the SEM, one electron beam scans the sample line by line, and four detectors each catch a different signal.
Secondary electrons show the powder's surface. Backscattered electrons show the section's pores and cracks. X-rays give the elements, and diffraction gives each grain's orientation.
Every image here is simulated by the twin, for this alloy.
The network uses three of them: satellites on the powder, the section's pores and cracks, and the grain size. EDS only checks the composition.
Bars are heat treated, then pulled. The furnace profile here is only illustrative: the twin models the strength it leaves.
The curve is the twin's simulated record of the test, up to fracture.
Yield strength, 349 megapascals, and elongation, 10.1 percent, are the two numbers the network keeps.
For copper, a one-hour corrosion screen ranks the DED deposits, and thirty days in seawater come before a utility is known.
After an hour at rest, two quick scans give an early corrosion rate and a breakdown potential.
In immersion, the coupon is weighed on days 1, 3, 7 and 14. After any reading, the policy may stop it.
On day 30 it is cleaned and weighed: 16.6 micrometres a year.
Both campaigns share one lab. From here on, each step is an icon that lights up while it runs.
